nodes.title: What a repository is
nodes.explain: A repository is a folder whose full history Git keeps in a hidden .git folder. Every saved state of the files is a commit, and the history is the chain of commits back to the first one.

nodes.title: Stage and commit changes
nodes.explain: Git records changes in two steps: git add puts chosen changes in the staging area, and git commit saves exactly what is staged with a message. Small commits with clear messages make history easy to read and undo.

nodes.title: Work on a branch
nodes.explain: A branch is a movable name that points at a commit. New commits move the current branch forward, so you can try an idea on its own branch without touching main.

nodes.title: Merge a branch back
nodes.explain: git merge joins another branch's commits into the current one. When both sides changed the same lines Git stops with a conflict: edit the file to the version you want, add it and commit.

nodes.title: Push and pull with a remote
nodes.explain: A remote such as origin is another copy of the repository, usually on a server. git push sends your commits there, git fetch downloads new commits, and git pull fetches and merges them into your branch.

nodes.title: Undo safely
nodes.explain: git restore throws away uncommitted edits to a file, git revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one, and git reset moves a branch. Prefer revert for anything already pushed, because it never rewrites shared history.
